title: How much of success is luck? Using luck by treating every decision as an empirical test
summary: Jason Cohen argues that success is neither pure luck nor pure merit: good and bad luck swirl constantly, and what is not luck is how you use it. His practical answer is to treat every decision as an empirical test, measuring everything so you can keep what works and eject what doesn't.

principles.text: Both can be true: success rests on intentional choices and on luck. Don't deny either one.
principles.quote: In fact, I can pick any decision in the history of Smart Bear and the same rhetorical pattern appears: Success tied to something intentional, but also leveraging something lucky.

principles.text: Luck is constant, but how you use it is not luck.
principles.quote: Good luck and bad luck are constantly swirling around you. How you use it, is not luck.

principles.text: Success means using luck: exploiting the good and identifying and ejecting the bad.
principles.quote: Overall success in business doesn't only mean you "got lucky," it means you used luck, taking advantage of the good, identifying and ejecting the bad.

principles.text: Build measurement in so you can tell success from failure; otherwise luck alone controls your fate.
principles.quote: In fact, ensuring that we could measure the efficacy of individual print ads was also a choice. Had we not done this, we wouldn't have been able to distinguish success from failure, and then indeed our destiny would be controlled by luck alone.

principles.text: Treat every decision as an empirical test: try anything, measure everything, follow what works.
principles.quote: Your best bet for success is to treat all your decisions as empirical tests. Confidence and experimentation are not contradictory. Try anything, measure everything, and follow what works, even if that means changing everything.

principles.text: Ask how you knew an idea was right, not what inspired it. Learn how to think, not how to copy.
principles.quote: The wrong question is: "What inspired that idea?" The right question is: "How did you know when an idea was right?" Or even more specific: "How does one know whether a print ad is working?"
